claims.claim: Justin Alexander says the delve format artificially isolates the encounter from its context and so defeats its own purpose.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'Are We Really This Stupid?', The Alexandrian, 2011
claims.page: Are We Really This Stupid?, 'Isolated Encounters'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander asks publishers to trust DMs rather than pre-programming every monster's behaviour in the text.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'Are We Really This Stupid?', The Alexandrian, 2011
claims.quote: publishers can put a little more trust in DMs
claims.page: Are We Really This Stupid?, 'Encounters on the Fly'

claims.claim: Brendan of Necropraxis describes the dominant published format as areas written out in lengthy proper English prose.
claims.quote: Areas are described in lengthy, proper english prose.

claims.claim: Brendan of Necropraxis grants that well-written prose modules are pleasurable to read.
Brendan of Necropraxis says the same prose modules are cumbersome to use in play.
claims.quote: quite cumbersome to use in play

claims.claim: Brendan of Necropraxis objects that Courtney Campbell's outline key, though usable, lacks poetry.
Brendan of Necropraxis keeps running prose but bolds the features the referee needs immediately.
claims.quote: I bold the immediately relevant features.

claims.claim: Brendan of Necropraxis faults boxed text for separating a thing's first impression from its elaboration further down the page.
claims.quote: separated the initial impression (“treasure chest”) from elaboration

claims.claim: Brendan of Necropraxis says the aim of bolding is that the referee can take in the area with a glance.
claims.quote: take in the area with a glance

claims.claim: On his worked example Brendan of Necropraxis reports the text that must be read is cut by more than half without degrading the prose.
claims.quote: cut down by more than half

claims.claim: Reviewing a 2006 DCC module, Gabor Lux says much boxed text and follow-up writing are expended to say relatively little.
claims.source: Gabor Lux (Melan), '[REVIEW] Halls of the Minotaur', Beyond Fomalhaut, 2018
claims.quote: much boxed text and followup writing are expended to say relatively little

claims.claim: Gabor Lux reports that the same module played better at the table than it read on the page.
claims.source: Gabor Lux (Melan), '[REVIEW] Halls of the Minotaur', Beyond Fomalhaut, 2018
claims.quote: It really did play better than it reads

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch's rule in a 2026 review is that read-aloud should never be long.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of 'The Swan Hollow Intrigue', tenfootpole.org, 2026

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch says long read-aloud makes players lose focus and reach for their phones.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of 'The Swan Hollow Intrigue', tenfootpole.org, 2026
claims.quote: Long read-aloud causes players to loose focus

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch says long passages set in italics are cognitively hard to read.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of 'The Swan Hollow Intrigue', tenfootpole.org, 2026
claims.quote: Long italics is hard to read, cognitively.

verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched live (HTTP 200, browser UA), stripped to text. Section 'ISOLATED ENCOUNTERS': quote word for word; the 'defeats its own purpose' limb is carried by the next sentence, 'This tends to fatally sabotage the entire point of the delve format to begin with', and the context limb by 'Attempting to isolate a tactical encounter from the context in which that tactical encounter occurs'. Post dated January 10th, 2011.

verdicts.trueWording: I think publishers can put a little more trust in DMs.
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section 'ENCOUNTERS ON THE FLY'. Quote verbatim inside 'I think publishers can put a little more trust in DMs (and, as DMs, we can put a little more trust in ourselves).' The pre-programming limb is supported throughout: the boardgame is 'forced to provide a “program” for each monster', the delve encounters have monsters 'pre-selected, pre-positioned, and pre-programmed', and the Helga example is offered against 'a pregenerated tactical map ... with accompanying text telling the DM' where to place minis.

verdicts.trueWording: Areas are described in lengthy, proper english prose.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim. 'Dominant published format' limb supported by the same paragraph: 'The most common style in published modules (and also probably the oldest ...) is the dreaded wall of text' and 'Unfortunately, this has become the accepted format for modules.' Post is by Necropraxis/Brendan (he signs comments 'Brendan Post author').

verdicts.trueWording: Modules in this format can be pleasurable to read (if well-written).
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim as a substring of that sentence on the raw page; the concessive framing ('can be ... but are quite cumbersome') matches the claim's 'grants'.

verdicts.trueWording: but are quite cumbersome to use in play
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the raw page, in the same sentence as the concession verified at 712, and about the same wall-of-text prose modules ('They just don’t work very well in play').

Quote verbatim. Usability limb: 'This method works admirably in terms of direct, in-game usability. However ... it has two flaws.' The page names the format only as 'Courtney’s “set design” hierarchical outline format', hyperlinked to hackslashmaster.blogspot.com/2012/06/on-set-design.html (Courtney Campbell's Hack & Slash); the surname itself is not printed on the page, so the expansion rests on that link, not on page text.

verdicts.trueWording: When I am writing new area keys, I bold the immediately relevant features.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. 'Keeps running prose' limb supported: the approach 'can be applied to existing modules without requiring rewriting', the worked Tower of Mouths example is bolded prose, and the saving is claimed 'without degrading the quality of the prose' — explicitly set against outline formats, which he says are unpleasant to read.

verdicts.trueWording: Boxed text is also flawed because it separated the initial impression ... from elaboration
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim including the curly quotes around “treasure chest”. 'Further down the page' limb supported by the parenthesis that follows: 'the contents are usually buried somewhere three paragraphs down the page, with no obvious connective element'.

verdicts.trueWording: A referee can take in the area with a glance
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, in the paragraph reading the bolded Tower of Mouths example — 'the immediately important features are clearly offset' — so the 'aim of bolding' limb is the sentence's own subject.

verdicts.trueWording: The amount of text that must be read ... has been cut down by more than half without degrading the quality of the prose.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Every limb present in that one sentence: text that must be read, cut by more than half, no degrading of prose quality; and it is stated of the worked Tower of Mouths (Matt Finch, Knockspell 3) example, with the caveat that this was 'already a rather short description, and the savings yielded are usually greater'.

verdicts.trueWording: much boxed text and followup writing are expended to say relatively little
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200). Quote is word for word once the source's mid-sentence line wrapping is normalized: 'It always feels like the encounters are overwritten – much boxed text and followup writing are expended to say relatively little'. Module identified on the page as 'DCC #35A: Halls of the Minotaur (2006) by Harley Stroh', review dated 20 March 2018. Byline reads 'Melan'; 'Gabor Lux' is not printed on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: It really did play better than it reads
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the same raw page. The table/page contrast is explicit: the review says it 'will also contrast how the module reads vs. how it was run by our GM', the play was a convention DCC game, and 'Fairly standard areas took on a character they didn’t have in the text I read later.'

verdicts.trueWording: Read-aloud should never be long and italics should never be long.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim as the first half of that sentence. Post 'The Swan Hollow Intrigue', posted September 5, 2026 by Bryce Lynch, reviewing Dylan Hyatt's Shadowdark adventure — date and reviewer as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: Long read-aloud causes players to loose focus and pull out their phones.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, including the page's 'loose' for 'lose'. Both limbs — losing focus and reaching for phones — are in that one sentence, reinforced by 'They don’t pay attention.'

verdicts.trueWording: Long italics is hard to read, cognitively.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the same raw page, immediately after the read-aloud sentence; the claim's 'long passages set in italics' matches the antecedent 'There are long stretches of read-aloud, in italics.'
